script: IT told me I didn't understand the systems, so I stopped fixing them. The store learned what I actually did.. I worked at a gas station as a manager. I was the guy you called when a store across state lines was short‑staffed, or if they needed help with paperwork and/or training employees. I was a staff lead on track to go to their IT department, until a company bought them out. I was, at the time, basically an assistant manager without handling money, that was until the promotion. The store was in the red, and they saw how I turned one store around when there was no manager, and the district manager (DM) handled the money. So, they moved me to this new store and just preached about the benefits. I took it, and from there is how this all happened. I am not a genius, but I do some Linux dev in my free time. I had a side job repairing computers, building machines from parts people ordered. I document everything (important later). The routine was paperwork, safe, bank, schedules. I flipped between black and red, then finally got all in the black consistently—took a couple of years. The equipment was the worst. Gas pumps, the server, the registers, the office computer—all aging. We defragmented the office PC a few times, the card readers would glitch, the server would just say "Not today," the registers would break after an update, pumps had BIOS errors. The commander—yeah, that thing—controlled every single device in the store. When something broke, we had to file an IT ticket; they picked who had it worst. Two guys, 30 stores. It would be weeks before they came. I didn't like that. So I fixed them myself. The server down? I rebooted it. Office PC down? I patched it. Registers giving errors? I rebooted the power strip. Soda machine down? I swapped the fuse. Card readers? I reset them. I never took anything apart; I was just band‑aiding the real issues. One day, I was called to train a new manager at a different store. My DM would handle my store while I did this. The DM didn't train them because it wasn't her area; they thought I was the better fit. I did it because the same walls for 70+ hours a week gets tiring. While training, I got a call, then another, then another. They asked why the card readers, registers, pumps were down. I told them the commander was frozen, so the whole system wouldn't allow card transactions. I reset it, and boom, it worked again. That's how I earned my reputation. Fast forward two weeks. The head of IT and maintenance emailed me. They said from now on I had to put in the form to get things fixed. I, of course, emailed them back that if I do that and they don't come out soon enough, the store will lose money. They said, and I kid you not, "You do not understand how complex these systems are, any 'fix' you do could damage them." That last comment irked me a bit. I didn't understand them? The guy who has been fixing things and pleading for updated systems for months does not understand them? Ok, fine. I told them I would comply.
